title: HTTP Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of http fundamentals and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—requests and responses—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study http fundamentals with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you build network-facing code that handles timeouts, untrusted responses, and partial failure. In this lesson, focus on requests and responses and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Network operations can fail, stall, or return untrusted data even when local code is correct. Validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and restrict retries to operations where repeating the request is safe. Apply that reasoning specifically to requests and responses and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect requests and responses with http methods before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Validate request construction and response handling separately from actual network execution. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: extend the example for http fundamentals to validate input and report a useful failure state. Keep network activity optional and use explicit timeouts before making a real request.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.

summary: HTTP Fundamentals is best understood by connecting its contract to a small observable example.

Use official versioned documentation and tests to confirm assumptions before relying on behavior in a larger application.
